title: Opinion: 4 Approaches to Keep Students from Offloading Their Thinking to AI
summary: One in 10 American teenagers say they complete all or most of their schoolwork with the help of artificial intelligence chatbots. These are the findings of a recent survey by the Pew Research Center among students aged 13–17. The output generated by AI can be so convincing that teachers are not always able to distinguish […]
content: One in 10 American teenagers say they complete all or most of their schoolwork with the help of artificial intelligence chatbots. These are the findings of a recent survey by the Pew Research Center among students aged 13–17. The output generated by AI can be so convincing that teachers are not always able to distinguish it from work written by a human. In a study conducted among nearly 300 teachers, experienced staff correctly identified AI-generated essays in only 37.8% of cases. This study was carried out two years ago. Imagine how much easier it has become for students to tailor their answers to the required tone and format of an assignment using the latest AI models. If a student can delegate to a neural network the intellectual work that the assignment was intended to encourage, the task itself becomes a mere formality. But I’m convinced that banning the use of AI isn’t the solution. Even when the answer is available instantly, an assignment can be structured in such a way that the students still have to do the bulk of the work themselves. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter Below are four approaches to designing this kind of assignment that my curriculum team and I have developed for the network of schools I founded. Make the lesson topic more personal for the student Every teacher knows this: If students are not interested in the topic, then they will only learn enough to get a passing score on a test. And if you can get any answer within a second from an AI, then why go deeper? Therefore, I always encourage our teachers to frame the lesson topic around the student; I call this technique “placing the student inside the story.” AI can easily answer “Why did Caesar cross the Rubicon?” But it can’t deal with a task in which the student is the protagonist: “Imagine you were in Caesar’s shoes. What would you do?” To answer this question correctly, the student will have to work out the situation himself: think about what was happening and what each option would lead to. AI could also answer on Caesar’s behalf, but then the teacher can ask the student to explain the reasoning behind their decision. Add an oral presentation to the assignment For decades, the main way to assess how a student thinks has been through essays; it was believed that by developing an argument on paper, they demonstrate their reasoning and understanding. But, as I mentioned at the start, AI has made great strides in essay writing. This does not mean I am suggesting we ban AI while carrying out a task. It can be useful — for example, to draw up a plan or gather material. However, in my opinion, real learning takes place during discussions and presentations, when students explain their conclusions aloud. This is where tricky questions come in handy. For example: Why did you use this argument, or which fact had the greatest influence on your conclusion? When answering such questions, the student is not simply repeating material they have learnt, but is linking facts and arguments, drawing on memory. The aim of the oral defense is not to catch students using AI, but to give them the opportunity to demonstrate they understand their own work. Since students have been using AI to prepare for class, I’ve noticed time and again that those who worked through the material on their own answer the teacher’s or the class’s questions with ease, whereas those who simply read back the generated text find it noticeably more difficult. Creating something that can be used Previously, in our programming classes, students started with the simplest practice programs: For example, they would write a few lines of code to display the phrase Hello, World! on the screen. Such tasks introduced students to the programming language, but it took quite a while for them to get to something that could actually be used. What’s more, writing code can easily be delegated to AI. We’ve changed the assignment: Now students use AI to create a working prototype, such as a video service with several features. I’ve noticed that in this format, they start adding things to their product that nobody asked for, simply because they want their creation to work better. This is where I see one of the most interesting possibilities for generative AI in education. Now students can produce a first version more quickly and learn by developing it further. And, most importantly, basic skills do not become any less important — they now have a clear purpose. Students are more likely to study a new subject not because it is on the syllabus and is compulsory, but because without it they will not be able to bring their idea to fruition. Setting micro-tasks during the lesson Instead of one large task, which is easy to delegate to AI, teachers can set lots of short tasks during the lesson. A small task relating to what is happening in the lesson is too fiddly to give to AI. It’s easier to think it through yourself than to explain the context to AI. For example, you could ask a student to suggest the next step in solving a problem, to respond to a classmate’s argument and say whether she agrees or if there is a better option. A student can also be asked to predict the outcome of an experiment, or, after a new fact comes up, decide whether the initial answer still holds. Each of these questions requires a modest but independent intellectual effort. Such micro-tasks do not make the use of AI impossible — nor is that the aim. They prevent students from handing all the work over to the machine and disengaging from the process. No matter how technology develops, one thing will always be up to us. Сoming up with a question that children will want to answer for themselves. A machine can suggest anything, but only a person can still spark a student’s interest.

title: 74 Interview: Karega Rausch Wants to Make All Indianapolis Schools Better
summary: Indianapolis has an aggressive new plan for how district and charter schools are governed, funded and held accountable, and is turning to someone with a long history with city charter schools to guide the shift. Karega Rausch, who helped create many of the city’s charter schools as head of the mayor’s Office of Education Innovation […]
content: Indianapolis has an aggressive new plan for how district and charter schools are governed , funded and held accountable, and is turning to someone with a long history with city charter schools to guide the shift. Karega Rausch, who helped create many of the city’s charter schools as head of the mayor’s Office of Education Innovation from 2007 to 2011, is back after 12 years with the National Association of Charter School Authorizers, the last six as president and CEO. He now returns as executive director of the Indianapolis Public Education Corporation , a newly-created board overseeing both the Indianapolis Public Schools and the city’s charter schools, who now serve more than half of the city’s students. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter Ordered by the state legislature, Rausch will guide that board in sharing taxes between charter and district schools, creating a busing system, and taking control of all school buildings in the city to make sure they serve students, whether as district schools or charter schools. The board is also starting on another mandated task — setting new academic standards to rate district and charter schools to help guide decisions about which schools should close, be overhauled or be replicated around the city. It’s not an easy task. IPEC and Rausch now have many powers that used to belong to IPS’ elected school board, a shift that has drawn complaints that rich charter school backers are damaging the district. The district is considering closing six schools as part of $20 million budget cuts after a tax voters passed this month gave all its new money to charters while just maintaining district revenue. There’s also debate over the future of Innovation Schools — a unique partnership in which the district covers a mix of busing, building and utility costs for 30 charter schools whose test scores count toward the district’s overall rating. The district is seeking to slash those subsidies — between $12 million and $60 million a year, depending on estimates — to save money. But Rausch told The 74’s Patrick O’Donnell in an interview earlier this month that he wants to raise standards for all Indianapolis schools, both district and charter. And he believes passage of the tax shows residents can support efforts to help both kinds of schools. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. The 74: Leaving a national position, a pretty fairly prominent position within the charter community, to come and do something that’s local. That’s a pretty big change. Why did you feel that was important to do? Rausch: I was really grateful and loved the work that we were doing at NACSA for a long period of time. I loved the difference that we were making, loved the impact that we were having. But the combination of essentially coming home, and being able to take some of the information and some of the knowledge gleaned from my work at NACSA over 12 years, and bring that here to do something really different and potentially transformative for kids and families, that was the biggest pull. People sometimes equate national influence as being better than local influence. I’ve never thought about it that way. I’ve always thought about it as ‘where you can do the most good and have the most impact. That’s in addition to really thinking about ways we can potentially break down some of the divides that exist in public education, so that we can figure out some new pathways for all kids to get something different and better. That was extraordinarily appealing to me. How do you think Indianapolis compares to other cities in terms of school choice and options available for parents? Indianapolis has stood out from a lot of other markets, because of really strong and growing student outcomes in the public charter space, especially for students of color and lower income kids — students that typically aren’t provided a lot of the same kind of opportunities. I think Indianapolis’s strong focus on generating really positive student outcomes is what I think can differentiate us from some other charter markets. I think there is a really great opportunity to continue to grow great public schools, irrespective of governance type, that I think can benefit even more kids. What I think is promising, is there are individual schools of both public school governance types that are doing really good work. That provides us an opportunity to stop talking about how public charters writ large are doing, how district schools writ large are doing and actually start looking at individual schools and seeing how well they’re advancing to outcomes. We can get away from the Us versus Them as much as we can, and really think about the systems needed so that we get more great schools, irrespective of governance type. There’s lots of talk that IPS needs to right-size, they need to scale back, and that they’ve got some schools that aren’t doing well and probably need to be closed. Are there charters in the city that aren’t doing the job well too that should be closed? We’ve got all kinds of schools that are doing great work, and some that are not. And those schools that are not doing well, it doesn’t matter what kind of a school it is. It needs to dramatically transform, or it needs to stop serving kids so that others who are doing well can do it. That comes from my background in charter school authorizing, where the whole deal was increased autonomy for accountability. That kind of ethos still has to be at play here, where yes, there are some great high-performing IPS schools, and there are some IPS schools that are struggling. There are some great charter schools and charter networks, and there are some that are struggling. We have to take an approach that treats all of those similarly when we are exercising accountability. So I think the direct answer to your question is yes. There are schools of all types that need to dramatically transform or stop serving kids. Do you think you’ll get huge pushback if it comes to that, if some charter schools need to close their doors? I don’t know if we get pushback on exercising equitable accountability for young people. That has to be the north star, irrespective of what folks may think about it. That’s also why part of IPEC’s work around a common school performance framework becomes really important. For the first time in our community, we can have a common understanding of what a high-quality school is and looks like, so that we can make decisions — on all schools of all types — that are doing great and need to be supported, potentially to serve more students, and schools that are not doing well need to dramatically transform or close. It’s still early, but how much leverage do you think IPEC has if you have an accountability system and schools aren’t meeting it? Do you have the teeth to make things happen? The authorizers have the final choice. There are a couple of things that are written in the statute. Yes, you are right, the decision-making around school transformation or closure rightly still rests right with authorizers and with the IPS school board. The law allows — if there’s a difference of perception around how schools are doing and need to close — that does give IPEC the ability to petition to the state board on those kinds of questions. But it’s our hope that we can build this common performance framework in a collaborative way, so that all parties are on the same page, so we don’t run into situations where we have disagreements, so we can be aligned on whether this school or this set of schools aren’t doing what they need to do, and we can collectively take action to make sure students are served better or differently. In terms of common performance frameworks, are there any cities that you think would be good models that you should really consider, or use as a base and adapt, or combine a couple? So I would point to some places that have pretty strong student outcomes as being potential markers, but we have to create something that is unique to Indianapolis. We should look at places like the State University of New York as a pretty high quality authorizer, with pretty strong student outcomes. The Massachusetts Department of Education has also been lifted up. Even the Indianapolis Mayor’s Office has been lifted up as a place for outcomes. But even as we look at some of these other places, we need to make sure that we are crafting something with key stakeholders in our community that is both acceptable and is rigorous. The part that I think is going to be really important is ensuring we don’t make excuses for low performance. That we demand and expect strong student outcomes is going to be critically important for this work. Otherwise, the work in creating the systems and conditions for young people to thrive will not be in service of the North Star. All of this has to be designed to get much stronger student outcomes. Are you an achievement level person or a growth level person? Indiana seems to be very proficiency focused, compared to other states that give schools credit for kids moving from not being able to read at all, to being able to read a little, then being able to read a little bit better. Both. You’ve got to have strong proficiency and got to have strong growth. Increasing proficiency will be important because that’s a marker of how well students are reading, writing and doing math at grade level. My desire and ambition is not just whether students are growing, but are they growing enough that they should get to proficiency within a few years? Sometimes I struggle with students growing at the same rate as their peers. That’s great, but if students are really far behind, we’ve got to find a way to accelerate that. Are students growing enough that they should be able to get to proficiency within a meaningful period of time? Are there any particular school models that you’ve seen and run across that are lacking in Indianapolis? That you think would be great to have here? I’ve been at this now for six weeks, as you know. Job one was working to get the (tax) referendum passed. So we’re now at a point where we can dig more deeply into these kinds of questions. We need to have lots of different kinds of models that young people are looking for and can help them grow and thrive. And we shouldn’t expand models just for models’ sake. It’s got to be models that fit needs and can still accelerate student outcomes, right? Having a common understanding of what success is is really important. IPEC is a very charter-heavy organization right out of the gate, in the number of people on the committee, the chair, and then the hiring of yourself. There are some folks who perceive your mission is to further charters more than the district and villainize this effort. What is your biggest message to parents and others with an interest in IPS? How should they view this whole effort? We need fantastic public schools of all types serving students well in Indianapolis. I didn’t take this job to destroy Indianapolis public schools, and I do not believe that the members of IPEC’s board are here to do that. We are here to try to create systemic coherence in a way that can generate more great outcomes for kids, and I will be the first to go on record to say, if we’ve got a district-run school, a charter school, or public charter school that is doing exceptional work and wants to serve more kids, we got to find a way to make that happen. So truly, this, from my vantage point, is not an effort to destroy anybody or anything. It is an effort to grow and to build more great options for young people. What’s your vision for how this city, the educational landscape of Indianapolis will be in five years? What’s your hope? Dramatically improved outcomes for everybody. That is the north star. Some may say it’s a little Pollyannish to say, but I believe that we can do this in a collaborative way, across public education, across public sectors. I think we have at least one proof point around how that would be, and that was the passing of the operating referendum that’s going to generate millions of dollars for all public school kids in the IPS boundary. The fact that it passed with 63% support is a really strong signal that our community is interested in all kids succeeding, not just one type of kid. This referendum had no new money for IPS. It was essentially continuing the tax they had before, then lots of new money for charters. Was that fair? I think that state law prescribed the way that this works, not just for Indianapolis,but for everybody across the state. You mean the state requiring new taxes to give the same dollars to every student at every school? That’s part of trying to get to a point of both clarity and equity amongst all public school kids. We were grateful that everybody came together to support that effort. Do you think IPS parents voted for this basically because ‘My kid’s school will sink if I don’t pass it? I don’t necessarily like money going to charters, but I don’t want the ship to go down?’ I wouldn’t want to speak for any families and what their motivations for this were. But I do think that, even if it was for different interests, the fact that we were able to come together and get this done is a positive thing. Do you think you’re going to be able to move fast enough to satisfy everybody? That’s a really good question. We’ll see. I don’t have a crystal ball on that right now, but yeah, we’ll see. There has been flare-up about the innovation schools and having to readjust lots of resources going to them. If IPS can’t financially support these schools anymore, are innovation schools really going to be a thing? Is there any point? So let’s see how negotiations play out. I’m optimistic that there are solutions the parties are working on to get to a point of preserving important relationships. But just on a base level, if IPEC takes charge of the buildings, and IPEC has control of transportation, that’s two of the biggest in-kind services that IPS was providing. IPEC itself, just existing, takes huge chunks out of what those contracts are. Does it make sense to have these arrangements anymore? When we come to a point of understanding what our facilities and transportation plans will be, sure, those relationships will look different than they do today. I think that’s a right, good, healthy, and inevitable kind of growth. What they look like and how those partnerships work will be important. I would just add, though, that for many of the innovation schools and IPS,there were contractual relationships, but there were also human being relationships that also exist that I think is important to preserve. Are there things about Indianapolis and this effort that you think other cities will eventually look to in the future as a model for themselves? We hope so. We hope that where there is a need for systemic coherence amongst lots of different kinds of public schools, that what we’re doing can serve as a way that can happen. We’re still a long ways from getting there, but we’re hopeful. What do you see as the biggest obstacles for your vision for things to come to fruition? There may be more as I spend more time than six weeks on the job, but the ones that seem to be emerging the most are navigating complicated relationships. There are people that have been working hard to advance multiple visions of what Indianapolis can and should be that sometimes collaborate well together sometimes don’t. Being able to navigate complicated relationships that have existed for a long time here is one that I wouldn’t necessarily characterize as an obstacle, but as an opportunity, you know, to bring folks together. But it’s going to be really hard to do. And then I would say, second, is for our community to understand what IPEC is designed to do and what it’s not designed to do. It’s important for folks to understand that teaching and learning remains in the purview of individual schools. That’s not a part of our role. We’re not going to be the ones that are determining curricula, or hiring and firing of school leaders or the superintendent. That’s not our role. There’s a lot of misperception on all sides,around what our role is. Any other message you would want to share to parents in this city about where you’re going and what you’re doing? It’s about stronger student outcomes. The work that we’re doing to create coherence has to result in stronger student outcomes for all young people. That is the north star in all of this, and that has to be what all public education in the Indianapolis Public Schools boundaries is measured by.

But it’s our hope that we can build this common performance framework in a collaborative way, so that all parties are on the same page, so we don’t run into situations where we have disagreements, so we can be aligned on whether this school or this set of schools aren’t doing what they need to do, and we can collectively take action to make sure students are served better or differently. In terms of common performance frameworks, are there any cities that you think would be good models that you should really consider, or use as a base and adapt, or combine a couple? So I would point to some places that have pretty strong student outcomes as being potential markers, but we have to create something that is unique to Indianapolis. We should look at places like the State University of New York as a pretty high quality authorizer, with pretty strong student outcomes. The Massachusetts Department of Education has also been lifted up. Even the Indianapolis Mayor’s Office has been lifted up as a place for outcomes. But even as we look at some of these other places, we need to make sure that we are crafting something with key stakeholders in our community that is both acceptable and is rigorous. The part that I think is going to be really important is ensuring we don’t make excuses for low performance. That we demand and expect strong student outcomes is going to be critically important for this work. Otherwise, the work in creating the systems and conditions for young people to thrive will not be in service of the North Star. All of this has to be designed to get much stronger student outcomes. Are you an achievement level person or a growth level person? Indiana seems to be very proficiency focused, compared to other states that give schools credit for kids moving from not being able to read at all, to being able to read a little, then being able to read a little bit better. Both. You’ve got to have strong proficiency and got to have strong growth. Increasing proficiency will be important because that’s a marker of how well students are reading, writing and doing math at grade level. My desire and ambition is not just whether students are growing, but are they growing enough that they should get to proficiency within a few years? Sometimes I struggle with students growing at the same rate as their peers. That’s great, but if students are really far behind, we’ve got to find a way to accelerate that. Are students growing enough that they should be able to get to proficiency within a meaningful period of time? Are there any particular school models that you’ve seen and run across that are lacking in Indianapolis? That you think would be great to have here? I’ve been at this now for six weeks, as you know. Job one was working to get the (tax) referendum passed. So we’re now at a point where we can dig more deeply into these kinds of questions. We need to have lots of different kinds of models that young people are looking for and can help them grow and thrive. And we shouldn’t expand models just for models’ sake. It’s got to be models that fit needs and can still accelerate student outcomes, right? Having a common understanding of what success is is really important. IPEC is a very charter-heavy organization right out of the gate, in the number of people on the committee, the chair, and then the hiring of yourself. There are some folks who perceive your mission is to further charters more than the district and villainize this effort. What is your biggest message to parents and others with an interest in IPS? How should they view this whole effort? We need fantastic public schools of all types serving students well in Indianapolis. I didn’t take this job to destroy Indianapolis public schools, and I do not believe that the members of IPEC’s board are here to do that. We are here to try to create systemic coherence in a way that can generate more great outcomes for kids, and I will be the first to go on record to say, if we’ve got a district-run school, a charter school, or public charter school that is doing exceptional work and wants to serve more kids, we got to find a way to make that happen. So truly, this, from my vantage point, is not an effort to destroy anybody or anything. It is an effort to grow and to build more great options for young people. What’s your vision for how this city, the educational landscape of Indianapolis will be in five years? What’s your hope? Dramatically improved outcomes for everybody. That is the north star. Some may say it’s a little Pollyannish to say, but I believe that we can do this in a collaborative way, across public education, across public sectors. I think we have at least one proof point around how that would be, and that was the passing of the operating referendum that’s going to generate millions of dollars for all public school kids in the IPS boundary. The fact that it passed with 63% support is a really strong signal that our community is interested in all kids succeeding, not just one type of kid. This referendum had no new money for IPS. It was essentially continuing the tax they had before, then lots of new money for charters. Was that fair? I think that state law prescribed the way that this works, not just for Indianapolis,but for everybody across the state. You mean the state requiring new taxes to give the same dollars to every student at every school? That’s part of trying to get to a point of both clarity and equity amongst all public school kids. We were grateful that everybody came together to support that effort. Do you think IPS parents voted for this basically because ‘My kid’s school will sink if I don’t pass it? I don’t necessarily like money going to charters, but I don’t want the ship to go down?’ I wouldn’t want to speak for any families and what their motivations for this were. But I do think that, even if it was for different interests, the fact that we were able to come together and get this done is a positive thing. Do you think you’re going to be able to move fast enough to satisfy everybody? That’s a really good question. We’ll see. I don’t have a crystal ball on that right now, but yeah, we’ll see. There has been flare-up about the innovation schools and having to readjust lots of resources going to them. If IPS can’t financially support these schools anymore, are innovation schools really going to be a thing? Is there any point? So let’s see how negotiations play out. I’m optimistic that there are solutions the parties are working on to get to a point of preserving important relationships. But just on a base level, if IPEC takes charge of the buildings, and IPEC has control of transportation, that’s two of the biggest in-kind services that IPS was providing. IPEC itself, just existing, takes huge chunks out of what those contracts are. Does it make sense to have these arrangements anymore? When we come to a point of understanding what our facilities and transportation plans will be, sure, those relationships will look different than they do today. I think that’s a right, good, healthy, and inevitable kind of growth. What they look like and how those partnerships work will be important. I would just add, though, that for many of the innovation schools and IPS,there were contractual relationships, but there were also human being relationships that also exist that I think is important to preserve. Are there things about Indianapolis and this effort that you think other cities will eventually look to in the future as a model for themselves? We hope so. We hope that where there is a need for systemic coherence amongst lots of different kinds of public schools, that what we’re doing can serve as a way that can happen. We’re still a long ways from getting there, but we’re hopeful. What do you see as the biggest obstacles for your vision for things to come to fruition? There may be more as I spend more time than six weeks on the job, but the ones that seem to be emerging the most are navigating complicated relationships. There are people that have been working hard to advance multiple visions of what Indianapolis can and should be that sometimes collaborate well together sometimes don’t. Being able to navigate complicated relationships that have existed for a long time here is one that I wouldn’t necessarily characterize as an obstacle, but as an opportunity, you know, to bring folks together. But it’s going to be really hard to do. And then I would say, second, is for our community to understand what IPEC is designed to do and what it’s not designed to do. It’s important for folks to understand that teaching and learning remains in the purview of individual schools. That’s not a part of our role. We’re not going to be the ones that are determining curricula, or hiring and firing of school leaders or the superintendent. That’s not our role. There’s a lot of misperception on all sides,around what our role is. Any other message you would want to share to parents in this city about where you’re going and what you’re doing? It’s about stronger student outcomes. The work that we’re doing to create coherence has to result in stronger student outcomes for all young people. That is the north star in all of this, and that has to be what all public education in the Indianapolis Public Schools boundaries is measured by.

title: Opinion: Anger Then Action: From Classroom Teacher to Investigative Reporter
summary: This essay first appeared on Alexander Russo’s The Grade When I walked into The 74’s newsroom on my first day in January of 2024, I couldn’t have known that an idea my editor would share with me would launch me on the hardest and most meaningful reporting of my career so far. The ask: to […]
content: This essay first appeared on Alexander Russo’s The Grade When I walked into The 74’s newsroom on my first day in January of 2024, I couldn’t have known that an idea my editor would share with me would launch me on the hardest and most meaningful reporting of my career so far. The ask: to look into New York’s 2019 Child Victims Act (CVA) and find out how many of the survivors who came forward to file civil claims alleged that they were sexually abused as children at or through their school? Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter Answering it would take more than two years — and require sorting through nearly 11,000 complaints filed in all 62 New York counties to identify which ones named a teacher, principal or other school employee as the alleged perpetrator. All told, I found nearly 2,000, or roughly 18% of the total number of complaints. Related New York Schools Named in Nearly 2,000 Child Sex Abuse Claims Two-thousand cases in which an adult, whose most important job was to educate and protect a child, was instead accused of violating and abusing them. More often than not, repeatedly. Countless times in which the system put in place to nurture kids instead shielded their abusers, a pattern that persisted over nearly 70 years. It’s a devastating number to sit with — and one that suggests child sex abuse in schools may be far more common than previously thought — and yet I also know, we’ve likely just scratched the surface. Every single one of the survivors I spoke with shared examples of lasting harm: addiction; agoraphobia; an obsessive need to constantly be moving and achieving; a complete lack of trust in institutions. Each of the alleged abusers I spoke with vehemently denied the allegations while also asserting they had left them all in the past. The survivors carried the pain, while their alleged abusers were free to move on. I knew I wanted to tell this story many years ago — before I even knew I wanted to be a journalist. It was a decade ago, and I was working as a high school English teacher. I anticipated from the start that teaching at this school would be extremely hard work, which it was. But I thought the hardest parts would be literacy instruction and handling the absurd, wonderful chaos that comes with a room full of 17-year-olds. I was not expecting to witness a deeply inappropriate relationship unfold between an adult man employed by my school, and one of our youngest, most vulnerable students. And to report it — time and time again. And to be ignored. I was in my early ’20s and still naively believed that the adults in charge of running the school would want to know about this. I believed they would be horrified by each new detail I uncovered — would jump to investigate it and ultimately hold this man responsible for the immense harm he was causing to a 14-year-old girl. But, like so many of the alleged abusers I came across in court filings, he was beloved by the school community. My repeated outcries were brushed aside and buried, and he was shielded. I have a vivid memory of eventually being told by a supervisor that “No one likes a whistleblower.” I felt so angry and helpless. I debated what to do next. Should I go to the police? To the state Department of Education? To a local news outlet? But I didn’t want it to become some salacious story told by a tabloid, and I felt like I didn’t have enough hard evidence to pursue any formal avenues on my own. So in the end I just kept reporting what I was seeing — kept logging incidents, kept filing complaints. We weren’t told anything. To my knowledge there was never any follow-up investigation. Seven years later, when I began my training as a journalist, a professor said that those who thrive in this field are the ones with “a low threshold for indignation.” I knew I not only wanted, but needed, to redirect my outrage and try to finally hold these systems accountable through investigative reporting. One reason we don’t know more about how prevalent sex abuse is in schools is because children don’t come forward in real time to report these crimes. What the Child Victims Act did was give adults the chance to go back into the past and tell these dark stories that they couldn’t when they were young. That created a trove of public court records — a decades-long accounting of alleged school sex abuse that I was able to access and report out. We’re often told to separate our emotions from our reporting, and to remain professionally detached to maintain impartiality. But for this project, I needed my anger to fuel me. My experience working in schools also grounded me. I would come across cases with truly horrific allegations of public and ongoing abuse, and I would have a moment in which I’d say to myself, “Simply how? How is it possible this went on and no one did a thing?” And then I’d remember what I’d seen. I’ve been asked what the hardest part of this project was, and it was the confluence of challenges that made it so grueling. First was the technical piece: scouring the New York State Courts Electronic Filing system, which — fellow reporters need not be told — is not the most user friendly. Once I identified cases, I had to read through thousands of pages of documents to determine if they met our standards for inclusion in the database. I spent hundreds of hours doing this. Then, there was the narrative piece. From the start, it was important to me that this story be told through the voices of survivors. But because of the trauma and shame that so often follows those who have experienced abuse, it is challenging to find people who want to go on the record with their stories. I spent endless days cold calling attorneys, reaching out to advocates, and interviewing experts. I eventually connected with one woman, who invited me into her home and generously shared her story over hours and days. Months before publication, though, she called me to tell me she had changed her mind. She was too scared to come forward because her settlement involved a non-disclosure agreement. If she told her story, something she deeply wanted to do, the school district that had shielded her alleged abuser had the right to counter-sue her. This was one of the hardest moments of all — as a reporter, but also as a human being. The anger I felt on this woman’s behalf — that she had been silenced for all of these years and now, her attempt at justice was silencing her once again — was overwhelming. I am incredibly grateful that a number of other survivors were ultimately comfortable having their stories shared. I spoke with one man who asked to remain anonymous because his adult sons had no idea what had happened to their father decades ago. His story, which is emblematic of so many I heard, became the lead to our piece. The afternoon before the story ran, I called this man’s attorney to prepare him for publication, and I learned devastating news: the man had died just weeks before, without ever seeing our story published or his case resolved. Once again, the system had failed him, moving too slowly to ever get this man anything approaching justice. The hope is that this story — and the journalism of so many others covering this issue — can help move the needle and lead to lasting institutional change so others don’t have to suffer the way he did. That’s why in some ways, the hardest part of this work is what comes next: The watching and waiting to see if after these years of work — and the decades of work of so many others — anything will change, either on a systemic level or an interpersonal one. In the weeks following publication, the U.S. Department of Education broadened a school sex abuse probe to include New York City public schools, citing our reporting. Though, as The New York Times swiftly pointed out, claims made by the administration appeared to include significant misreadings and misuse of our findings. And the department has simultaneously de-prioritized investigations into these very issues. Related U.S. Dept of Education Broadens School Sex Abuse Probe, Cites The 74’s Reporting Initial feedback also included emails and calls from advocates across the state and country who plan to use our investigation to advance legislation. But perhaps the most meaningful feedback has come from Jane Does who have reached out — a number of whom had cases that were included in our database. If a teacher sees a kid staying late with their colleague, in a dark classroom, door shut, day after day, will they investigate? Will they take evidence of abuse — no matter what form it comes in — and speak up? Will their administrators listen and step in? Or will they turn a blind eye because that feels like the easier, less messy thing to do in the moment? The answer here is not villainizing teachers. It’s empowering those who are bystanders to step in and protect kids. These complaints implicate every adult in the building from the principal to the janitor. Teachers are not solely responsible, nor are they the enemy. In fact, they are the first line of defense. They are the best shot kids have at protection when their colleagues cross boundaries and do harm. We have to give them the tools to do so. And when the systems fail, we must continue to report on them. My editor and I plan to continue reporting on this story in multiple ways and hope others also take the database we compiled and use it to localize the story and hold their own institutions accountable, so this cycle can be broken and the next generation of kids can be spared this trauma.

title: Doula Care Aiming to Improve Maternal Health and Wellbeing Grows in NC’s Rural Counties
summary: “I just don’t want to die having my baby,” a pregnant woman told her doula, Taya Partin, at their first meeting. Partin shared that memory at a doula training workshop in the Halifax County town of Enfield, where 14 women attended three days of intensive classes offered by N.C. Central University. Fear of death is […]
content: This article was originally published in NC Newsline. “I just don’t want to die having my baby,” a pregnant woman told her doula, Taya Partin, at their first meeting. Partin shared that memory at a doula training workshop in the Halifax County town of Enfield, where 14 women attended three days of intensive classes offered by N.C. Central University. Tara Partin, a doula enrolled in NCCU’s workshop, said she was able to calm a client who feared she would not live through childbirth. (Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline) Fear of death is a real worry for Black women who are pregnant. In North Carolina, Black women are 1.7 times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes, according to the state Maternal Mortality Review Committee report released last month. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter Death rates were highest among women who live in rural areas and in southeastern counties, the report said. Nearly nine in 10 deaths were preventable. NCCU’s training program was created to help provide doulas to rural counties where it can be hard for pregnant women to find care. Doulas provide non-medical support during pregnancy, labor, birth, and for a short time after babies are born. In recent years, efforts to integrate doulas into maternal care have expanded. Research has found that women who have doulas are less likely to have cesarean sections, have lower risks of preterm birth, and are less likely to be given a drug that speeds up labor. The continuous presence of doulas during labor helps reduce stress. Doulas help women in labor walk or change birthing positions, practices that help shorten labor. Doulas stay in contact with parents in the weeks after they bring their babies home, and can be the first to spot medical problems or signs of postpartum depression. The NCCU classes convene at the university’s Rural Health Hub headquarters in Enfield. The hub provides services aimed at improving the health of residents in low-wealth counties. Students in a doula training class sponsored by NC Central University use a small ball inside a balloon to demonstrate how the cervix thins during labor. (Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline) Undi Hoffler is the doula training program’s director. Inspired by her own experiences as a doula, she worked to add the training to NCCU’s work on rural health. The NCCU program recruits participants from rural counties in northeastern North Carolina. That region of the state has a cluster of counties the March of Dimes calls “maternity care deserts.” Those are counties without a medical professional that delivers babies or a birthing center or hospital that offers obstetric care. Some women in these rural counties may have to travel an hour or more to see an obstetrician or midwife, Hoffler said. Providing evidence-based information and emotional support to someone who is pregnant is “a tremendous resource,” she said. NCCU’s training represents one effort to build support systems for pregnant women in the state’s rural counties. Building community-based support for women’s health in Chatham A Chatham County nonprofit has similar goals, but is working to build a range of community services for women. EMBRACe (Equity for Moms and Babies Realized Across Chatham) helps provide doula training for Black women and Latinas, and is helping support a multi-cultural community-based doula cooperative called Abriendo Caminos that hosts bilingual childcare classes. EMBRACe started as a project of the Chatham County Health Department in response to health disparities. It was focused on bringing institutions together to address inequities, said Casey Hilliard, one of the co-founders. The organization is now a separate nonprofit that focuses on building and supporting community leaders to transform maternal care. The healthcare system too often fails when it comes to women’s health, she said. “We have the data and the experiences to prove that they’re not listening to us, they’re not seeing us,” Hilliard said. “So what we’re trying to do is to find ways to shift the money and the power and the resources into the spaces where care really does exist.” That means having doulas, community health workers, childbirth education and support groups, and paying birth workers to provide services to everyone who needs them, Hilliard said. At an EMBRACe retreat in October, some doulas said their own traumatic experiences drew them to the work because they wanted to help make births better for others. Liliana Nava at the EMBRACe retreat in Chatham County in October 2026. (Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline) Liliana Nava, who is in nursing school, said she endured a long, traumatic labor before giving birth to her daughter by C-section four years ago. Nava was at UNC, where a volunteer doula helped her with massages and encouragement. “She was able to ground me,” Nava said. “She talked to me in such a voice that I felt like she was soothing me to sleep.” The doula was able to impart a sense of calm that medical personnel and Nava’s partner could not. “Being a doula is just making a difference for somebody else and making them feel like they’re not alone,” she said. Chatham County has a relatively high Latino population. More than half of Siler City’s population is Latino. That makes it important for some pregnant women to find fluent Spanish speakers for support. Omayra Pumalpa started EMBRACe’s childbirth education classes in Chatham and has attended births as a doula. “Most of the pregnant women in the immigrant community don’t even want to go to the doctor because they don’t know what they’re going to find,” she said. Federal law requires video interpretation in medical offices and hospitals, but it can be an imperfect solution. Pumalpa said she has attended births with teenagers and women who would otherwise have been alone. At least once, the family was afraid of ICE and didn’t want to come to the hospital. content: This article was originally published in NC Newsline. “I just don’t want to die having my baby,” a pregnant woman told her doula, Taya Partin, at their first meeting. Partin shared that memory at a doula training workshop in the Halifax County town of Enfield, where 14 women attended three days of intensive classes offered by N.C. Central University. Tara Partin, a doula enrolled in NCCU’s workshop, said she was able to calm a client who feared she would not live through childbirth. (Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline) Fear of death is a real worry for Black women who are pregnant. In North Carolina, Black women are 1.7 times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes, according to the state Maternal Mortality Review Committee report released last month. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter Death rates were highest among women who live in rural areas and in southeastern counties, the report said. Nearly nine in 10 deaths were preventable. NCCU’s training program was created to help provide doulas to rural counties where it can be hard for pregnant women to find care. Doulas provide non-medical support during pregnancy, labor, birth, and for a short time after babies are born. In recent years, efforts to integrate doulas into maternal care have expanded. Research has found that women who have doulas are less likely to have cesarean sections, have lower risks of preterm birth, and are less likely to be given a drug that speeds up labor. The continuous presence of doulas during labor helps reduce stress. Doulas help women in labor walk or change birthing positions, practices that help shorten labor. Doulas stay in contact with parents in the weeks after they bring their babies home, and can be the first to spot medical problems or signs of postpartum depression. The NCCU classes convene at the university’s Rural Health Hub headquarters in Enfield. The hub provides services aimed at improving the health of residents in low-wealth counties. Students in a doula training class sponsored by NC Central University use a small ball inside a balloon to demonstrate how the cervix thins during labor. (Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline) Undi Hoffler is the doula training program’s director. Inspired by her own experiences as a doula, she worked to add the training to NCCU’s work on rural health. The NCCU program recruits participants from rural counties in northeastern North Carolina. That region of the state has a cluster of counties the March of Dimes calls “maternity care deserts.” Those are counties without a medical professional that delivers babies or a birthing center or hospital that offers obstetric care. Some women in these rural counties may have to travel an hour or more to see an obstetrician or midwife, Hoffler said. Providing evidence-based information and emotional support to someone who is pregnant is “a tremendous resource,” she said. NCCU’s training represents one effort to build support systems for pregnant women in the state’s rural counties. Building community-based support for women’s health in Chatham A Chatham County nonprofit has similar goals, but is working to build a range of community services for women. EMBRACe started as a project of the Chatham County Health Department in response to health disparities. It was focused on bringing institutions together to address inequities, said Casey Hilliard, one of the co-founders. The organization is now a separate nonprofit that focuses on building and supporting community leaders to transform maternal care. The healthcare system too often fails when it comes to women’s health, she said. “We have the data and the experiences to prove that they’re not listening to us, they’re not seeing us,” Hilliard said. “So what we’re trying to do is to find ways to shift the money and the power and the resources into the spaces where care really does exist.” That means having doulas, community health workers, childbirth education and support groups, and paying birth workers to provide services to everyone who needs them, Hilliard said. At an EMBRACe retreat in October, some doulas said their own traumatic experiences drew them to the work because they wanted to help make births better for others. Liliana Nava at the EMBRACe retreat in Chatham County in October 2026.
